description.value: One cold winter night to find the deed that keeps Fernhill in the family.

config.value: …arrangements with the county bank, where the deed may rest secure until…

variants.text: You have nothing that would interest a cat of standing.
A slow blink. The account is already settled.
The kipper vanishes with terrifying efficiency, and something is decided about you. From now on, you have a shadow.
That has no appetite you can help with.
There's nothing to prune about that.
That doesn't wind.
The lane runs three dark miles to the village, and the cab is gone. You are not leaving without what you came for.
The glass door to the folly path is sealed fast under a rind of frost. Nothing short of real warmth in these pipes will shift it.
The wind comes off the downs and worries at the bare limes.
A gust rattles every pane in the greenhouse at once.
The wind drops for a moment, and the night is very quiet.
Far off in the village, the church bell counts another quarter hour gone.
The cold finds you the moment you step out, and means it.
The cold again, familiar now.
You step out of the wind, and your ears sing in the sudden quiet.
The house holds its old hush — mothballs, cold ash, and wax.
Mrs Kettle does not move from the study door. "The study is not for visitors," she says, to her knitting.
Mrs Kettle turns the bottle to read the label, and something in her shoulders comes down an inch. "Her ladyship's oloroso. Well." She steps away from the study door. "Five minutes, mind."
"Her walking coat. Twenty winters old and warmer than anything you could buy now. She'd not begrudge you the loan of it tonight."
"Shut since the spring, and it'll stay shut. Unless," she looks at you over the needles, "you were to bring me something that made the evening kinder."
Tobias turns his head and spits, which appears to be his whole opinion on the subject.
"She's not dead, just cold. Fill her, set the valve, then light her — in that order, mind, or she'll clank at you like church bells."
Tobias goes very still when he sees it. "Her little silver box. She wore it the night of the fire and never after. Whatever it opens, it's up at the folly."

The lantern stops swinging. "Twenty years I've not opened that door, and her ladyship neither." He looks up the dark hill for a long moment. "Go on then, if you must. The door's only warped, not cursed. Shoulder it."
"Bank?" He snorts. "Bank never had it. Her ladyship trusted banks the way foxes trust hounds."
You twist the dial and the boiler answers with a hollow CLANK, like church bells dropped down a well. Cold, dry iron. The brass plate insists: FILL. PRIME. LIGHT.
You crank the stopcock a hard quarter-turn.
The plunger sinks with a dry wheeze and comes up again. Nothing to prime — the jacket is empty.
Somewhere inside the iron, water gurgles down into the jacket.
The plunger meets resistance at last and thumps home. The boiler is primed.
Flame catches with a soft whump, and within moments the pipes begin to tick and stretch as warmth crawls toward the greenhouse.
The warped door's first draught in twenty years drags across the floor — and wakes a thread of sparks in the old blasting cord. The fuse is burning toward the cache.
The fuse hisses on, eating its slow way toward the fireworks.
Sparks walk the waxed cord, closer now.
It is racing you.
The shears bite through the waxed cord. The spark train staggers, gutters, and dies a hand's breadth from the cache.
The cache goes up in one white roar, and the folly keeps its secrets after all.
Somewhere beyond the grounds the last light goes out of the sky. Midnight is coming on.
Somewhere back in the vaults, a drop falls.
Drip. The dark keeps its own time.
Something small skitters away from your lamplight and is gone.
Bare-fingered pinching will mangle it. This wants the garden shears.
It is all stem and hope — nothing to prune yet. What it wants is warmth in these pipes.

You take the dead growth off in three clean cuts, and the vine answers the warmth almost while you watch: a single heavy fruit swells, splits — and something small and silver slides out into the leaf mould. Verity's own way of banking.
The vine has given everything it kept.
At the warm end of the greenhouse staging, something green stirs.
The little brass door wants its crank key — the kind a careful housekeeper leaves in a coat pocket.
It is wound and walking. Tick, tock.
The key turns, the weights climb, and the old clock clears its throat and begins to walk again: tick, tock, after twenty years.
The case clock counts the quarter, bright and even, through the whole house.
The poker has been drinking the furnace's heat — it would take the skin off your palm.
Smoke pads after you, unhurried, as if it were her own idea.
Smoke pads down the staging, ignores the vine entirely, and noses hard at the leaf mould at the warm end. Cats know where things are buried.
— and over it Verity's photograph, which you cannot stop looking at now
The small hours settle over Fernhill. Dawn — and the auction — are no longer an abstraction.
Grey light finds the gates, and with it the first motorcar of the auction party. Whatever Fernhill still hides, it will hide it for strangers now.

You come down the drive with the deed of Fernhill inside your coat, and the iron gates, for the first time tonight, look like they are holding the world out rather than you in. At dawn the hammer will fall on nothing: the proof came out of the fire after all.
The warped door doesn't shift. Twenty years of weather have set it like a jaw — and something in you doesn't care to force Verity's folly without knowing more of it.
The weathervane creaks the same one story it always tells, whatever the hour.
The house has stopped listening for your footsteps.
Somewhere below, a door you have never opened settles on its hinges, as if it had been waiting to be yours.
Wrought-iron gates stand open on one hinge apiece, rust freckling the scrollwork. The gravel drive runs north toward the dark shape of the house.

The cab is already grinding away down the lane, its lamps swallowed by the dark. An auction notice is nailed to the left-hand gate, ruffling in the wind: FERNHILL HOUSE AND GROUNDS, BY ORDER OF THE ESTATE, AT DAWN.
The drive curves between bare lime trees, gravel crunching underfoot. The house looms ahead to the north; the gates are back south.

A paved court before the front door, holding a dry fountain crusted with last summer's leaves. The greenhouse glimmers palely to the west; a squat brick shed hunches to the east; the front door of the house is north.
Glass panes furred with frost on both sides. Staging benches run the length of the house, and a door in the north wall — glass too — leads up toward the folly, if it would open.
Brick, low, and bitter with old coal dust. The estate's boiler sits cold as a tomb against the back wall, its pipes running off through the earth toward the greenhouse.
The hill rises behind the greenhouse, and on its crown stands the folly: a little stone temple, fire-scarred about the windows, that nobody has entered in twenty years.
Soot still ghosts the walls in here, twenty years on. The night sky shows through a scorched hole in the dome, and a cache of ancient estate fireworks slumps against the far wall.

The heart of the house: a cold marble floor, a dead fireplace under a wide mantel{mantel-hint}, and a tall case clock standing silent against the stairs. Doors lead west to the study and east to the kitchen; a colder passage runs north.
Verity's study, exactly as she left it: a desk under the window, a travelling trunk against the wall, and the smell of pipe smoke that never quite left the curtains.
Copper pans hang in ranks over the cold range. The pantry door stands in the north wall.
Narrow shelves of preserves and crockery. With the door shut, no one in the kitchen would know you were here.
A bare landing at the top of the cellar steps. An oil lamp sits in a wall niche, left where a careful hand could always find it.
Brick vaults run off into the dark, cold enough to keep milk in July. Somewhere back in the blackness, water is dripping.
A stone-framed door of oak, warped and silvered by the fire. It has not been opened in twenty years.
A plain white-painted door with a bolt on the pantry side.
A heavy grey door, locked as long as anyone can remember. The keyhole is tarnished black.
A bristle mat worn bald in the middle, older than you are. It sits a little proud of the flagstone, as if something kept it from lying flat.
A small key gone black with weather.
A hurricane lamp with a full reservoir and a clean chimney.

A cast-iron estate boiler, cold now, its dial at rest. Pipes run from its flank toward the greenhouse. A stopcock and a primer plunger stand ready on its flank, and a small brass plate reads: FILL. PRIME. LIGHT. IN THAT ORDER.
A quarter-turn stopcock on the feed pipe from the rain tank.
A long-handled primer plunger, worn smooth by fifty winters of use.
The letter that brought you here: Fernhill goes to auction at dawn, and whatever Great-Aunt Verity hid is lost with it unless someone finds the deed tonight.
"…the property known as FERNHILL to be sold at public auction at first light. Any party asserting prior title must produce the original deed of the estate before the fall of the hammer."
Verity's old travelling trunk, papered with steamer labels from ports she never mentioned. The lid is heavy but unlocked.
A page torn from a diary, the hand young and furious.

"K. says the greenhouse will take the worst of the frost and the vine with it. Let it. What matters is safe where the fire went, and only the little silver thing will open it. If I cannot keep Fernhill, no bank and no buyer shall have the proof of it."
Only the middle of the letter survived its trip through a grate. It seems to say the deed went to the bank in town. It seems to.
A wide stone mantel over the dead fireplace, dusted but bare except for a single framed photograph.
Verity at thirty, on the folly steps, squinting into some summer long gone.
Knowing what the diary knows, you see it now: the folly whole behind her, and on her knee a small steel box with a bright slot in its lid.
A great grey wool overcoat hanging by the door, too heavy for anyone's shoulders but hers. The pockets are deep.
A small brass crank key — the kind that winds a tall case clock.
A forge-made crowbar, cold and certain.
A pine crate nailed shut hard, stencilled FERNHILL ESTATE — BOILER SPARES.
A wooden-handled tin opener, estate issue.
A four-spoked brass handle, sized for the boiler's water valve.
A flat tin of kippers with no ring-pull and no mercy.
One bronze kipper, pungent enough to summon any cat in the county.
Long-bladed garden shears, oiled and sharp — Tobias's pride, judging by the edge.
A dusty bottle of oloroso, the good stuff, hidden behind the pans at hip height where a housekeeper might know to look.
Verity's vine, at the warm end of the staging over the buried pipes: barely more than a seedling now, twenty years after the frost that should have killed it.
Since the pipes warmed it has thrown a spray of hurried white flowers along every cane.
Its one heavy fruit has come and gone; the pruned canes lie quiet against the glass.
A smoke-grey cat with lantern eyes, appointed to the pantry mice and answerable to no one.
A long iron poker for the furnace grate.
A long waxed fuse snaking from the fireworks cache across the floor. Old, but not too old to burn.
A small steel box under a shroud of soot, unmarked but for a neat bright slot in the lid — the exact size of a locket that does not open like a locket.
Heavy paper, folded in oiled cloth, whole and legible after twenty years in the dark: the original deed of Fernhill.
"…the house and grounds known as FERNHILL, held in perpetuity by the family and heirs of the bearer of this instrument."
The housekeeper, planted before the study door with her knitting and no intention of moving. Her eyes say the study is not for visitors.
The groundskeeper, out in all weathers on his rounds, a storm lantern swinging at his knee. Weathered, watchful, in no hurry to help.
A little silver locket on a fine chain, its face engraved with the folly before the fire. It is heavier than it looks, and it does not open like a locket.
Cold, underslept, and the last of the family who still believes Verity hid the deed.
Fresh print on old iron: FERNHILL HOUSE AND GROUNDS, BY ORDER OF THE ESTATE, AT DAWN.
"Sale to be conducted at the property at first light. Viewing by arrangement with the solicitors, Messrs. Hobbes & Vane."
Bare pollarded limes, planted two lifetimes ago, creaking in the wind.
A dry stone basin drifted with last summer's leaves. The cherub in the middle has lost his nose to some hard winter.
Slatted staging the length of the glasshouse, empty but for one determined vine at the warm end, over the buried heating pipes.
Lagged iron pipes leaving the boiler's flank, running toward the greenhouse through the earth.
Cold ash and a firedog, under the wide stone mantel.
A tall case clock, stopped at some hour years gone. The winding hole waits behind the little brass door in its face.
A leather-topped desk under the window, its blotter still dented by a heavy hand.
Floor-to-ceiling curtains of faded bottle green, deep enough to swallow a person whole.
Ranks of copper pans, dull with disuse but hung in strict order.
A black iron range, cold to the wrist, its fire door hanging open.
Narrow shelves of preserves in ranked jars: damson, quince, and things gone too dark to name.
A little arched niche worn smooth at the lip — a lamp has lived here a long time.
The folly's little dome, breached by fire; the night sky shows through the black-edged hole.
An iron weathervane on the gatepost, older than the house behind it.
The vane swings hard north, as if the night had opinions.
The vane holds north. Of course it does.
A book must never win this line.
The vane noses the evening breeze, unhurried.
The vane sits easy in the last of the light.
Nor this one.
The vane keeps its own counsel.
